picked.t: Asia Pacific faces growing health challenges as population ages
picked.body: Asia Pacific's rapidly aging population is creating economic opportunities while placing growing pressure on healthcare systems, prompting calls for greater investment in disease prevention and healthy longevity. The challenges were discussed at the Silver Economy Forum 2026, held at the Kuala Lumpur Convention Centre on Nov. 11-12. Organized by the Global Coalition on Aging (GCOA) and the Malaysian Healthy Ageing Society (MHAS), the event brought together policymakers, business representatives and healthcare experts to discuss how countries can support longer, healthier and more productive lives. Nearly 1.3 billion people in Asia Pacific, or about a quarter of the region's population, are expected to be aged 60 or older by 2050. Globally, people aged 60 and above account for an estimated US$19 trillion in annual consumer spending, projected to reach US$34 trillion by 2036. However, realizing this economic potential will depend partly on whether older people can remain healthy and economically active. Research by the Economic Research Institute for ASEAN and East Asia (ERIA) in Vietnam and the Philippines found that 30-50% of older people were still working. Among those who had stopped, about half cited health problems. Dr. Liem Nguyen, ERIA's program manager for social welfare, said discussions about the silver economy should go beyond older people's purchasing power. "It is not just about savings and how older people are spending money, but it is about employment for older people," Nguyen said. He identified health conditions, financial insecurity and gaps in social protection as barriers to older adults remaining in the workforce. Closing the gap between longer lives and healthier lives Against this backdrop, Bayer hosted a media discussion titled "Longer Lives, Better Years: Reimagining Healthcare for Asia Pacific" in Kuala Lumpur on Nov. 11, focusing on chronic diseases and the importance of early intervention. "Asia Pacific is going through one of the fastest demographic shifts in the world. We need to make sure that longer lives are also healthier lives," said Simon Rosof, head of Bayer Pharmaceuticals' Asia Pacific region. "That means finding disease earlier, treating it effectively, and recognizing prevention as an investment in people, health systems, and economies. The time to act is now." The challenge is reflected in the widening gap between life expectancy and healthy life expectancy. A Global Burden of Disease study published in The Lancet Public Health in July 2026 found that people worldwide spend an average of 10.7 years in poor health, up from 8.8 years in 1990. The gap widened in 203 of the 204 countries and territories studied. Across Asia Pacific, people reaching 60 can expect to spend nearly five of their remaining years living with disease or disability, according to figures presented at the forum. "Most people think aging is about living longer. The real challenge is staying healthier for longer," said Dr. Maria Borentain, global vice president and head of cardiovascular and renal clinical development at Bayer. She stressed the importance of early diagnosis and appropriate treatment in helping older people maintain their independence and quality of life. Non-communicable diseases account for nearly 90% of deaths in the World Health Organization's Western Pacific Region, according to figures cited at the event. Risk factors including high blood pressure, high cholesterol and elevated blood sugar can be detected through routine health checks. Malaysia's 2023 National Health and Morbidity Survey found that about one in three adults had high cholesterol, with more than half unaware of their condition. Bayer encouraged adults over 40 to monitor their blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar, and seek medical advice when necessary. Tackling the growing burden of stroke Stroke was highlighted as a major health concern as populations age. Asia accounted for 61% of global stroke deaths in 2020, or approximately 4.1 million deaths. The annual toll is projected to reach 6.6 million by 2050, representing 69% of the global total, according to figures cited by Bayer. High blood pressure is a major stroke risk factor, while diabetes can further increase the risk. Preventing another stroke is also a key part of long-term care for survivors. Bayer cited research indicating that 10-16% of stroke survivors experience another stroke within a year. Borentain highlighted an international clinical trial published in The New England Journal of Medicine in April 2026. It involved more than 12,000 patients across 37 countries, including over 3,500 participants from Asia Pacific, and examined a new approach to preventing recurrent stroke. Beyond its impact on patients, stroke carries substantial economic costs. picked.t: Inside the suite Kim Jong-un stayed in during his Hanoi visit
picked.body: Melia Hotel on Ly Thuong Kiet Street opened in 1999 to become one of the capital’s first five-star properties. For the 2019 summit, the North Korean delegation booked six of the hotel’s 22 floors comprising nearly 100 rooms. A delegation first surveyed the property on Feb. 19 before the first group checked in on Feb. 22. Photo by Melia Situated on the 22nd floor, the presidential suite is the hotel's most opulent accommodation. It is where Kim stayed from Feb. 26 to March 2. Designed in bright, neoclassical style, the suite has large arched windows offering panoramic city views. A 25 sq.m dining room doubles as a meeting area for up to 10 people. Kim’s delegation requested a private kitchen area for their own chefs and food supplies for the leader. Adjacent to the living area is a desk corner for brief discussions or personal work. The private quarters include an 85 sq.m bedroom featuring a king-sized bed and automated curtains, leading into an adjacent dressing room. While strict security protocols, restricted access zones, and coordination with security forces were enforced throughout the visit, the hotel management said everything continued almost entirely normally for other guests. The classic European-inspired bathroom has marble finishes, a circular Jacuzzi tub, and high-end amenities, including a Dyson hair dryer and Balmain bath products. Photos by Giang Huy

picked.t: Ho Chi Minh City's future financial hub gets 4 major roads underway
picked.body: The section of Tran Bach Dang between the Nguyen Co Thach intersection and the Tran Nao roundabout is taking shape six months after construction resumed. Around 300 m of the road is being paved with asphalt. The 55-m-wide route will have six lanes. Workers and heavy machinery are preparing the roadbed, installing drainage systems and compacting the surface. Contractors are carrying out multiple construction activities simultaneously to meet the year-end completion target. Workers and heavy machinery are preparing the roadbed, installing drainage systems and compacting the surface. Contractors are carrying out multiple construction activities simultaneously to meet the year-end completion target. The central median, sidewalks and lighting systems are also being upgraded and completed along the route. Around 2 km of Tran Bach Dang, from the Nguyen Co Thach intersection to the Thu Thiem Tunnel entrance, remains closed to traffic despite being largely completed several years ago. Once the unfinished sections are connected, the road will provide a continuous route through the Thu Thiem New Urban Area, improving connectivity and easing traffic pressure on Mai Chi Tho and Nguyen Co Thach streets. Adjacent to Tran Bach Dang is the construction site of To Huu Street and part of Luong Dinh Cua Street. The intersection between the two routes is temporarily fenced off for construction. The other two roads, Bui Thien Ngo and Nguyen Thien Thanh, were largely completed nearly 10 years ago but still see little traffic as they have yet to be fully connected to Tran Bach Dang and To Huu streets. The four key roads, alongside other infrastructure projects, are expected to help transform the Thu Thiem New Urban Area into a modern financial, commercial and service hub for Ho Chi Minh City. Graphics by VnExpress/Hoang Thanh
